Understanding Go Concurrency

By Jane Developer on March 1, 2026

Go's concurrency model is one of its most powerful features. Built on the concept of communicating sequential processes (CSP), Go provides goroutines and channels as first-class language primitives for concurrent programming.

Goroutines

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime. You create one by prefixing a function call with the go keyword:

go func() {
    fmt.Println("Hello from a goroutine")
}()

Goroutines are incredibly cheap — you can easily run thousands or even millions of them. The Go scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads efficiently.

Channels

Channels are typed conduits through which you can send and receive values. They provide synchronization between goroutines without explicit locks:

ch := make(chan int)
go func() { ch <- 42 }()
value := <-ch

Select Statement

The select statement lets a goroutine wait on multiple channel operations. It's like a switch statement but for channels:

select {
case msg := <-ch1:
    fmt.Println("Received from ch1:", msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
    fmt.Println("Received from ch2:", msg)
case <-time.After(1 * time.Second):
    fmt.Println("Timeout")
}

Best Practices

  • Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating
  • Use context.Context for cancellation and timeouts
  • Always handle goroutine lifecycle — avoid goroutine leaks
  • Prefer channels for coordination, mutexes for state protection

For more details, see the official concurrency guide and the Go blog post on pipelines.
